items.title: Fake Recall Texts Want Your Card
items.summary: Scammers are texting and emailing that something you bought was recalled for safety and that you are owed money back. Tap the link and it asks you to sign in or type a card number — that is the whole trick, and it is spreading fast right now. Real recalls never arrive as a link in a surprise message. Check the product yourself, free, at cpsc.gov/recalls, or open the store's app and look at your orders. My rule is simple: don't click, check it yourself.

items.title: Your hard drive warns you before it dies — CrystalDiskInfo is the free health checker at crystalmark.info
items.summary: Download CrystalDiskInfo free from crystalmark.info (it's the Crystal Dew World site), open it, and look at the big word at the top of the window. A blue Good means your drive is healthy. A yellow Caution or a red Bad means it's on its way out, and you should copy your pictures and documents off it today. It's free, it works with no internet connection, and reading it takes about a minute.

items.title: Using the same password everywhere? Google's free Password Checkup at passwords.google.com/checkup finds the weak ones
items.summary: Open your browser and go to passwords.google.com/checkup. Sign in with your Google account and click Checkup. It shows you every saved password that is too weak, reused on more than one website, or already leaked in a data breach — and it walks you through changing each one, site by site. It's free, it's built into your Google account, and there's nothing to download.

items.title: An Emergency Apple Fix for a Flaw Hackers Are Already Using
items.summary: Apple rushed out an emergency update this week for a flaw hackers are already using against Apple computers. The fix stops a harmful file — one you might open from an email or a download — from running hidden code. The real repair is free from Apple, so ignore any pop-up telling you to call a number; that is a scam. It takes two minutes: open the Apple menu, click System Settings, then General, then Software Update. I've seen computers sit months behind — please update today.

items.title: Chrome now asks before opening an unsafe website — update yours free at chrome://settings/help
items.summary: Chrome is turning on a safer way to browse this month: it tries the secure version of a site first, and if the site can't do secure, it stops and asks you before opening it — you'll see a warning instead of walking in blind. To be sure you have it, open Chrome, click the three dots in the top-right corner, then Help, then About Google Chrome. It updates itself in about a minute. Not sure you have Chrome? Go to google.com/chrome and click Download. Free, from Google.

items.title: ChatGPT is now free inside Microsoft Word — get the add-in free at chatgpt.com/apps/word or Word's Insert > Get Add-ins
items.summary: Open Microsoft Word, click Insert at the top, then Get Add-ins, and search ChatGPT to install it — free. (You can also go to chatgpt.com/apps/word and click Install.) A ChatGPT panel appears on the right side of your document. You can ask it to fix a sentence, shorten a paragraph, write a first draft of a thank-you note or a complaint letter, or explain a word in a contract. You only need a free ChatGPT account, and the free plan includes a set amount of use each month.

items.title: A Fake \"You're Invited\" Email Is the New Way In
items.summary: Scammers are breaking into regular email accounts and sending fake invitations — a birthday party, a fundraiser, a wedding — from someone you actually know. Click "view the invitation" and it asks you to sign in with Google, Apple, or Microsoft; that login screen is fake, and the password you type goes straight to the crooks. A real invitation never asks you to log in just to see it. I tell folks to check with the sender by a quick call first.

items.title: Firefox just got a cleaner new look that can tuck your tabs down the left side — update free at firefox.com
items.summary: Open Firefox, click the Menu button (the three lines in the top-right corner), then Help, then About Firefox — it checks for the new version and installs it for you in about two minutes. Don't have Firefox yet? Go to firefox.com and click Download; it's free and it's made by Mozilla.

items.title: Someone using your Google account? Google's free Security Checkup at myaccount.google.com/security-checkup shows every device signed in
items.summary: Open myaccount.google.com/security-checkup in your browser, sign in with your Google account, and follow the short list it shows you. It reviews the devices signed in to your account, the apps that have access to it, and any password it thinks is weak or reused — and it walks you through fixing each one. No download, no cost, about two minutes.

items.title: A 'New Plastic Medicare Card' in the Mail Is a Scam
items.summary: An official-looking plastic Medicare card is landing in mailboxes, with a phone number to "activate" your new benefits — and that call is the whole scam. Real Medicare cards are paper, and nobody from Medicare will ever call, text, or email asking for your Medicare, Social Security, or bank number. Don't ring a number printed on the letter — type medicare.gov into your browser yourself, or use 800-633-4227, the number I check before I trust it. Already shared it? Report it at ftc.gov.

items.title: Is your email in a data breach? Check free in seconds at haveibeenpwned.com and turn on alerts so a scammer never gets there first
items.summary: Open haveibeenpwned.com in your browser, type your email address in the box, and click the button. It is free, it takes about ten seconds, and you do not have to create an account or hand over a password. Then scroll down the page and click Notify me, so it sends you an email the day your address shows up in a future leak.

items.title: Tired of ads following you everywhere? Brave is the free browser at brave.com that blocks them by itself — nothing to add, nothing to pay
items.summary: Go to brave.com and click the Download button, install it, and then use it exactly like your current browser. Brave blocks ads and the trackers that follow you from site to site on its own, the moment you install it. You do not add anything, you do not change any settings, and you never pay a cent.
